query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using in situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) enables direct, time-resolved observation of oxide phase formation and phase stability in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys during oxidation, thereby providing a more detailed understanding of transformation kinetics compared to post-mortem analyses.
generation.material_initial_state: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA sample to high-temperature oxidation under controlled atmospheres (e.g., vacuum and air).
generation.conditions: Temperatures in the range of approximately 800–1200 °C with controlled exposure times and defined atmospheric conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The gradual formation of oxide phases (such as spinel and halite oxides) on the alloy surface that evolves over time.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, oxygen interacts preferentially with certain elements (e.g., Mn) in the HEA, leading to the nucleation and growth of oxide phases. HTXRD can capture the time–temperature-dependent evolution of these phases, thereby linking oxidation kinetics to phase stability.
generation.predicted_outcome: HTXRD measurements will reveal a clear evolution of diffraction peaks corresponding to emerging oxide phases and potential phase transformations in the alloy lattice, thus correlating oxidation kinetics with phase stability changes in real time.
generation.baseline: Traditional post-mortem sample analyses that cannot capture transient phase transformations during high-temperature oxidation.
generation.boundary: This method is specifically validated for HEAs with oxidation behaviors similar to CrMnFeCoNi and within the highlighted temperature and atmospheric conditions; its applicability to other alloys and extreme conditions remains to be investigated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative correspondence between HTXRD patterns and thermodynamic predictions (e.g., CALPHAD outcomes) needs further validation; the influence of specific oxidation kinetics on phase stability is not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples and perform in situ HTXRD measurements during controlled high-temperature oxidation (both in vacuum and in air). Concurrently, analyze similar samples using traditional post-mortem techniques. Compare the time-resolved diffraction data with thermodynamic predictions from CALPHAD.
measurements: Time-resolved XRD patterns showing the emergence and evolution of oxide phase peaks.
Quantitative phase analysis over oxidation time.
Comparison of observed phase formation kinetics with CALPHAD thermodynamic predictions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in situ HTXRD does not reveal distinct, time-dependent phase changes (i.e., if the diffraction patterns do not show the expected evolution of oxide phases or if they are inconsistent with both CALPHAD predictions and post-mortem analyses), then the hypothesis that HTXRD is an effective method to capture high-temperature oxidation-induced phase transformations is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. First reported in 2004 [ [1] ], high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys comprising five or more elements in equal or nearly equal molar fractions, with each element present at a mole fraction of approximately 5–35 at.% [ [2] ]. The presence of multiple elements leads to a high configurational entropy, resulting in solid-solution structures with face-centred cubic (FCC) and body-centred cubic (BCC) lattices, rather than intermetallic compounds [ [3] ]. In recent years, HEAs have garnered significant consideration in the field of materials science because of their exceptional performance characteristics, including high strength [ [4] ], corrosion resistance [ [5] ], soft magnetic properties [ [6] ], high hardness [ [7] ], wear resistance [ [8] ], fatigue resistance [ [9] ], and softening resistance at high temperatures [ [10] ]. The superior high-temperature behaviour of HEAs can be attributed to four underlying effects: the high entropy effect, the sluggish kinetic diffusion effect, the severe lattice distortion effect, and the cocktail effect [ [11] ].
